summaryEn: A steel fabricator that reinvented itself as the company holding up Taiwan's offshore wind farms — welding 2,000-tonne, 90-metre steel jackets at Taipei Port, with more than NT$50bn of orders running to 2029. The backlog is real; so is its total dependence on government auction rounds.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + press; offshore-wind framing — the NT$50bn+ backlog to 2029, the 21 Hailong jackets delivered, the Phase 3-1 order and the doubling of monthly jacket capacity credited, but extremely lumpy project-based quarterly earnings, FY2025 EPS slightly below FY2024 despite the boom, operating cash flow well below net profit, and complete dependence on Taiwan's offshore wind auction timetable stated plainly; sector Steel → Offshore Wind Foundations & Steel Structures)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Century Iron & Steel (世紀鋼鐵結構, TWSE: 9958) builds the steel structures that stand on the seabed and hold offshore wind turbines above the Taiwan Strait. Founded in **1987** as a steel-structure fabricator for buildings and bridges and **listed in March 2008**, it made a bet a decade ago that has defined it: that Taiwan would build an offshore wind industry, and would require the foundations to be made locally.

The physical scale is the first thing to understand. A **jacket foundation** is a lattice steel tower — Century's are **over 90 metres tall and weigh around 2,000 tonnes each** — fabricated at **Taipei Port**, loaded onto vessels and installed on the seabed, where it must survive typhoons, earthquakes and salt water for twenty-five years. Very few facilities anywhere can weld and handle structures of that size, and building one requires a deep-water port, enormous cranes and years of qualification.

The order book reflects the position. Century holds **more than NT$50bn of offshore wind foundation orders extending to 2029**. Its subsidiary completed and delivered **21 three-leg jackets for the Hailong offshore wind project** — a milestone for Taiwan's wind localisation policy — and in **July 2025 signed for 35 jackets for the Phase 3-1 Haikuo wind farm (495MW)**, following a 2024 contract for another field. New capacity at **Taipei Port Phase 5** and the "Qingtian Tower" facility, from the second half of 2025, lifts **monthly jacket output from four units to eight**.

The financials show a business in a strong phase. Gross margin has run from **11.2% (2024Q4) to 33.2% (2026Q1)**, operating margin from **5.9% to 28.8%**, and **2026Q1 EPS of NT$2.63 was up 87%** on a year earlier. Monthly revenue has accelerated to **+64%** most recently. Trailing **return on equity is 12.19%**, dividends have risen to **NT$4.5**, and at **NT$105.00 the shares trade on 13.4× earnings and 2.26× book with a 4.29% yield**.

Two cautions belong up front. This is **project revenue, and it is extremely lumpy**: 2024Q1 earned **NT$2.66** per share and 2024Q4 earned **NT$0.40**, on the same order book — recognition timing, not performance. And despite the boom, **FY2025 EPS of NT$6.56 was slightly below FY2024's NT$6.95**. **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$577m also fell well short of NT$1.04bn of net profit**, the normal working-capital pattern of a project business but worth watching.

Above all, **the entire backlog rests on Taiwan's offshore wind auction rounds proceeding**. The honest read: **a genuinely rare industrial capability with a multi-year backlog and excellent current margins — whose demand curve is drawn by government policy.**

Century Iron & Steel was founded in **1987** doing conventional work: fabricating **structural steel for buildings and bridges**. It was a competent, unremarkable business in a competitive industry, and it **listed in 2008**.

The transformation began with a policy decision it did not make. Taiwan committed to building **offshore wind capacity in the Taiwan Strait** — one of the best wind resources in the world, and one of the most difficult places to build in, with typhoons, earthquakes and a seabed that demands engineered foundations rather than simple monopiles. Crucially, the government attached **localisation requirements**: developers awarded capacity had to source significant components from Taiwanese suppliers, deliberately creating a domestic industry rather than importing complete wind farms.

**Jacket foundations** were among the hardest items to localise. A jacket is a welded lattice structure — Century's are **more than 90 metres tall and about 2,000 tonnes** — that must be fabricated to offshore standards, moved without deforming, shipped, and installed on the seabed to survive twenty-five years of salt water and storms. Building them requires a **deep-water port site, enormous fabrication halls, heavy-lift cranes, certified welders and international qualification** — capital and capability that cannot be assembled quickly.

Century built it, at **Taipei Port**, and became Taiwan's dominant supplier. The proof point came when its subsidiary **completed and delivered 21 three-leg jackets for the Hailong project**, an outcome widely treated as the milestone of Taiwan's offshore wind localisation programme. The order book has since grown to **more than NT$50bn running to 2029**, with **35 jackets contracted in July 2025 for the Phase 3-1 Haikuo wind farm**, and capacity is being doubled — **from four jackets a month to eight**.

It is a genuine industrial transformation: a general steel fabricator became one of a small number of companies in the world that can build these things. It is also a business whose customers exist because a government decided they should.

- **1987 (9 Oct)** — Century Iron & Steel founded as a structural steel fabricator for buildings and bridges.
- **2008 (12 March)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (9958)**.
- **2010s** — Taiwan commits to offshore wind in the Taiwan Strait with **localisation requirements**; Century invests in **jacket foundation** capability at **Taipei Port**.
- **2020–2021** — Dividends of **NT$2.98** and **NT$2.99** as early wind work begins.
- **2022** — A weak year: **FY2022 EPS NT$1.59**, including a Q4 loss; dividend falls to **NT$0.49**.
- **2023** — Recovery: **FY2023 EPS NT$4.45**; dividend **NT$2.91**.
- **2024** — **FY2024 EPS NT$6.95**, though quarterly results swing from **NT$2.66 (Q1) to NT$0.40 (Q4)**; dividend **NT$4.16**. Contract signed for a further wind farm's foundations.
- **2025 (July)** — Subsidiary signs to supply **35 tubular jackets for the Phase 3-1 Haikuo offshore wind farm (495MW)**.
- **2025 (H2)** — **Taipei Port Phase 5 and the "Qingtian Tower" facility** come on stream, lifting **monthly jacket capacity from 4 to 8 units**. **FY2025 EPS NT$6.56**; dividend **NT$4.5**.
- **Milestone** — Century Wind Power **completes and delivers 21 three-leg jackets for the Hailong offshore wind project**, each over **90 metres tall and 2,000 tonnes** — a landmark for Taiwan's wind localisation.
- **2026Q1** — **EPS NT$2.63, up 87% year-on-year**; gross margin **33.2%**, operating margin **28.8%**; monthly revenue up to **+64%**. Backlog **above NT$50bn, extending to 2029**.

Century's accounts show **a project business in the strong part of a cycle, with the volatility that implies**.

- **Earnings that jump around by quarter, and should be read annually.** Annual EPS: **NT$1.59 (FY2022) → 4.45 (FY2023) → 6.95 (FY2024) → NT$6.56 (FY2025)**, with **2026Q1 at NT$2.63, up 87%**. Within FY2024 the quarters ran **NT$2.66, 2.19, 1.70, 0.40** — a six-fold spread caused by **revenue recognition timing on long projects**, not by performance changing.
- **FY2025 was slightly below FY2024 despite the boom.** **NT$6.56 against NT$6.95.** With the order book growing and capacity doubling, that is a useful reminder that backlog is not revenue and revenue is not profit — the timing of project milestones governs the reported year.
- **Margins are currently excellent.** Gross margin: **11.2% (2024Q4) → 24.7% → 34.3% → 26.5% → 31.2% → 33.2% (2026Q1)**. Operating margin: **5.9% → 28.8%**. A 28.8% operating margin on heavy steel fabrication reflects scarcity — there are very few alternatives for this work in Taiwan.
- **Cash lags profit.** **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$577m** against **NT$1.04bn of net income**. Project businesses tie up working capital in materials and work-in-progress ahead of milestone payments, so this is expected — but with capacity doubling it is worth monitoring.
- **A solid balance sheet with heavy investment.** **NT$49.4bn of assets** on **NT$24.8bn of equity** — a **49.9% debt ratio** — with a substantial **NT$14.8bn of cash**. The Taipei Port Phase 5 and Qingtian Tower expansion is being funded from this base.
- **A dividend that tracks the projects.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$0.99 (2019) → 2.98 → 2.99 → NT$0.49 (2022) → 2.91 (2023) → 4.16 (2024) → NT$4.5 (2025)**. The **4.29% yield** at NT$105.00 is attractive — and the **NT$0.49 paid for 2022** shows what a weak project year does to it.
- **Trailing return on equity is 12.19%**, and the valuation is **13.4× earnings and 2.26× book** — moderate for a company with a backlog running to 2029.

The financing reality: **strong current profitability and a genuine multi-year backlog, in a business whose reported earnings depend on when steel gets delivered rather than on how the year went.**

**Stance: a rare heavy-fabrication capability with more than NT$50bn of offshore wind orders running to 2029, earning a 28.8% operating margin at 13.4x earnings — and entirely dependent on Taiwan's wind auction timetable.**

The bull case:

1. **A capability very few companies have.** Fabricating **90-metre, 2,000-tonne jacket foundations** requires a deep-water port site, heavy-lift infrastructure, certified offshore welding and international qualification. Century built it at **Taipei Port** and delivered **21 jackets for the Hailong project** — the proof that it works at scale.
2. **Visibility to 2029.** **More than NT$50bn of orders**, including **35 jackets for the Phase 3-1 Haikuo wind farm (495MW)** contracted in July 2025. Very few manufacturers of any kind have a five-year backlog.
3. **Localisation policy protects the position.** Taiwan requires developers to source domestically, which is precisely why Century exists as a wind supplier — and why foreign fabricators cannot simply undercut it.
4. **Capacity doubling into the demand.** Taipei Port Phase 5 and the Qingtian Tower facility lift **monthly output from 4 to 8 jackets**, with margins currently at **33.2% gross / 28.8% operating** and a **4.29% yield**.

The counter-arguments:

- **The demand curve is drawn by the government.** Taiwan's offshore wind programme has proceeded through auction rounds whose timing, pricing and developer participation are policy outcomes. Delays and withdrawals in offshore wind have been common internationally, and a backlog is only as firm as the projects behind it.
- **Project accounting makes any single period unreliable.** **FY2024 quarters of NT$2.66, 2.19, 1.70 and 0.40**; and **FY2025's NT$6.56 was below FY2024's NT$6.95** despite a growing order book.
- **Cash trails profit.** **NT$577m of operating cash flow against NT$1.04bn of net income** in 2026Q1, while capacity expands.
- **Doubling capacity is a bet.** Eight jackets a month must be filled beyond the current backlog for the investment to pay.

An **infrastructure-backlog** thesis: excellent current economics and rare capability, held with the understanding that the customer is ultimately the state's energy policy.

Century sells **very large welded steel structures**, and its economics are those of heavy project fabrication:

- **Jacket foundations (the core).** A lattice steel tower — Century's are **over 90 metres and around 2,000 tonnes** — that sits on the seabed and supports an offshore wind turbine. Taiwan's seabed and typhoon conditions favour jackets over simpler monopile foundations, which is why this specific, difficult product is the one required. Each is fabricated at **Taipei Port**, load-out onto installation vessels, and installed offshore.
- **Traditional steel structures.** The original business — buildings, bridges, industrial plant — which continues alongside and provides a base load for the fabrication halls.
- **How revenue is recognised, and why the quarters swing.** Contracts run for years and revenue is booked against **project progress and delivery milestones**. A quarter in which several jackets complete looks spectacular; a quarter of fabrication in progress looks weak. That is why **2024Q1 earned NT$2.66 and 2024Q4 earned NT$0.40** with nothing fundamental changing.
- **Why the margin is high right now.** Gross margin at **33.2%** and operating margin at **28.8%** on structural steel is unusual, and reflects **scarcity rather than technology**: Taiwan's localisation rules require domestic foundations, and the number of facilities capable of building them is very small. Pricing reflects that.
- **The capacity question.** Output is rising **from 4 jackets a month to 8** with the Taipei Port Phase 5 and Qingtian Tower facilities. Because the cost base is fixed fabrication capacity, **utilisation is the profit driver** — and the doubled capacity needs projects to fill it.

The levers are **order intake from wind auction rounds, project execution timing, fabrication utilisation and steel input costs**. The strength is a physically rare capability protected by localisation policy, with a backlog to 2029. The vulnerability is that **the fabrication halls are fixed assets serving a demand stream created by government auctions** — and that when a wind round slips, there is no alternative customer to fill an 8-jackets-a-month facility.

Offshore wind is an industry built by policy, and its supply chain reflects that.

- **Why Taiwan built one.** The **Taiwan Strait has among the best wind resources in the world**, and Taiwan imports nearly all its energy. Offshore wind therefore serves both decarbonisation and energy security. The government structured development in **auction rounds** with **localisation requirements** — developers must source specified components domestically — deliberately creating a Taiwanese supply chain rather than importing finished wind farms.
- **Why foundations are the hard part.** Turbines and blades can be imported. **Foundations cannot practically be shipped from far away** — they are enormous, and transport costs and load-out logistics dominate. Taiwan's seismic conditions, typhoons and seabed require **jacket structures** rather than simpler monopiles, which are heavier, more complex and more welding-intensive. That combination makes local fabrication both necessary and difficult.
- **The competitive set.** Domestically, Century is the dominant jacket fabricator; **CSBC (2208)**, elsewhere in this collection, participates in offshore wind support work from a different angle. Internationally, European fabricators such as Bladt and Sif and Asian yards compete for projects outside Taiwan's localisation perimeter — which is precisely what the policy is designed to limit.
- **The industry's global reality check.** Offshore wind worldwide has had a difficult few years: **rising interest rates, cost inflation, cancelled projects and developers writing off investments**, particularly in the US and UK. Taiwan's programme has generally continued, but the international experience is a reminder that **awarded capacity is not built capacity**.
- **What comes next technically.** Fixed-bottom jackets suit shallower water; **floating foundations** are required for deeper sites and represent the next technical step for the industry and for anyone hoping to serve it.

Century's position is **strong and structurally protected inside Taiwan**. The industry truth is that **a supply chain created by policy is sustained by policy** — the localisation rules that made this company also mean its addressable market ends at Taiwan's territorial waters unless it can win work abroad.

**Strengths**
- **Rare heavy-fabrication capability**: 90-metre, 2,000-tonne jackets at **Taipei Port**, with **21 delivered for the Hailong project**.
- **Backlog above NT$50bn extending to 2029**, including **35 jackets for Phase 3-1 Haikuo (495MW)**.
- **Excellent current margins**: gross **33.2%**, operating **28.8%**; **2026Q1 EPS +87%**; monthly revenue **+64%**.
- **Protected by localisation policy**; **NT$14.8bn of cash** and a **4.29% yield**.

**Weaknesses**
- **Extremely lumpy project earnings** — FY2024 quarters ran **NT$2.66 → 0.40**.
- **FY2025 EPS NT$6.56 below FY2024's NT$6.95** despite a growing order book.
- **Operating cash flow NT$577m against NT$1.04bn of net profit** while capacity expands.
- **49.9% debt ratio** funding fixed fabrication capacity.

**Opportunities**
- Capacity doubling **from 4 to 8 jackets a month** at Taipei Port Phase 5 and Qingtian Tower.
- Later auction rounds and, technically, **floating foundations** for deeper water.
- Export fabrication work beyond Taiwan's localisation perimeter.

**Threats**
- **Auction-round delays or developer withdrawals** — common in offshore wind internationally.
- **Steel input cost volatility** on multi-year fixed-price contracts.
- Doubled capacity left underutilised if the project pipeline slows.

- **The demand curve is a government policy (the defining risk).** Century's wind business exists because Taiwan requires domestic sourcing and runs offshore wind auction rounds. Backlog above **NT$50bn to 2029** is genuine, but offshore wind projects worldwide have been **delayed, repriced and cancelled** over the past few years as interest rates and construction costs rose. Awarded capacity is not built capacity, and a slipped round has no substitute customer.
- **Project accounting makes single periods unreliable.** **FY2024's quarterly EPS ran NT$2.66, 2.19, 1.70 and 0.40**, and **FY2025's NT$6.56 came in below FY2024's NT$6.95** while the order book grew. Any conclusion drawn from one quarter — in either direction — is likely to be wrong.
- **Capacity is being doubled into a policy-dependent pipeline.** Monthly output rises **from 4 to 8 jackets**. Fixed fabrication capacity must be utilised; if the auction timetable slips, the cost base does not.
- **Working capital.** **NT$577m of operating cash flow against NT$1.04bn of net profit** in 2026Q1. Project businesses fund materials and work-in-progress ahead of milestone payments, and expansion increases that requirement.
- **Input cost exposure.** Steel prices move over the life of multi-year contracts; a fixed-price contract signed before a steel rally compresses the margin realised on it.
- **Geographic confinement.** The localisation policy that protects Century inside Taiwan also defines the boundary of its protected market. Growth beyond the current programme requires winning fabrication work internationally, against established European and Asian yards.

Century's outlook depends on **whether Taiwan's offshore wind rounds proceed on schedule and whether the doubled capacity gets filled.** The axes to watch:

- **Order intake from subsequent auction rounds.** The backlog above **NT$50bn to 2029** is the current asset; new orders determine what happens after. Any news of auction delays, repricing or developer withdrawal is the most important signal for this company.
- **Utilisation of the new capacity.** Monthly output is rising **from 4 to 8 jackets** with Taipei Port Phase 5 and Qingtian Tower. Because costs are fixed, utilisation drives the margin — currently **33.2% gross and 28.8% operating**.
- **Annual, not quarterly, earnings.** Project recognition makes quarters meaningless in isolation: **FY2024 ran NT$2.66 down to NT$0.40 across four quarters**. The FY2026 total against **FY2025's NT$6.56** is the meaningful comparison, with **2026Q1's NT$2.63 (+87%)** a promising start.
- **Operating cash flow converging with profit.** **NT$577m against NT$1.04bn** in 2026Q1. As deliveries complete and milestone payments land, the gap should close.
- **Work beyond Taiwan.** The localisation policy defines the protected market's edge. Any international fabrication contract would materially change the company's long-term ceiling.

Bottom line: Century Iron & Steel turned a conventional steel fabricator into **the company that physically holds up Taiwan's offshore wind farms** — **90-metre, 2,000-tonne jackets built at Taipei Port**, **21 delivered for Hailong**, **more than NT$50bn of orders to 2029**, capacity doubling to **8 jackets a month**, and current margins of **33.2% gross and 28.8% operating** at **13.4× earnings** with a **4.29% yield**. It is also a business whose **quarterly earnings swing six-fold on recognition timing**, whose **FY2025 came in below FY2024** despite the boom, and whose **entire demand stream is created by government auction rounds**. Judge it on **order intake and annual earnings** — a rare industrial capability, holding a backlog written by policy.
